description: HemoTrack is a multidisciplinary team developing a space-focused health monitoring concept to track hemolysis and red blood cell health in astronauts. Our project explores non-invasive breath carbon monoxide monitoring, personalized baselines, trend analysis, and early alerts. We are interested in biology, biomedical science, data analysis, software development, and user-centered design. We welcome creative collaborators who want to contribute to space health innovation.
summary:
HemoTrack is an exploratory software prototype designed to support the monitoring of red blood cell health during long-duration spaceflight. Inspired by NASA’s MARROW study, it explores longitudinal breath carbon monoxide (CO) monitoring while accounting for ambient CO levels.
Using synthetic data, HemoTrack establishes a personal baseline, tracks changes over time, applies a three-day rolling average, and flags sustained elevations for further review.
Developed in Google Colab using Python, the prototype demonstrates how personalized trend monitoring could support future astronaut health-monitoring systems.
All data are synthetic. HemoTrack is a research prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic system.
details:
HemoTrack is a proof-of-concept software prototype for longitudinal monitoring of potential changes in red blood cell destruction during spaceflight.

The system uses breath CO and ambient CO measurements to calculate a simplified CO difference. It then establishes a personal baseline using the first seven monitoring days and calculates deviations from that baseline. A three-day rolling average is used to identify sustained elevations. When the rolling average remains above an experimental threshold for three consecutive days, the system generates a review alert.

The prototype was developed in Google Colab using Python, Pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib. It includes synthetic data generation, trend analysis, alert logic, data export, and a visual monitoring dashboard.

Its main innovation is the use of personalized longitudinal trends rather than relying only on a single fixed measurement. This approach could inform the design of future astronaut health-monitoring software.

The current prototype uses synthetic data and does not include a physical sensor or clinical validation. The simplified breath-to-ambient CO difference is exploratory and does not reproduce the full NASA MARROW measurement protocol. Alerts indicate patterns for further review, not confirmed hemolysis.

AI Disclosure: ChatGPT was used as an assistive tool for code refinement, troubleshooting, and editing project text. It was also used to generate the closing visual, which is clearly identified as AI-generated. The project concept, research direction, and development decisions were guided by the team. All data used in the prototype are synthetic and do not represent real astronaut measurements.
